analysis.one_liner: Applies Social Security payroll taxes to income above $300,000 and lowers taxes on moderate retirees' benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have taxed earnings above $300,000 for Social Security, never got a hearing or vote before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, Social Security payroll taxes stop applying to wages above a yearly cap (about $127,200 in 2017), no matter how much someone earns. This bill would keep the tax on regular wages as-is, then apply the same tax again to income above $300,000 a year, and count those earnings slightly in the benefit formula. It would also raise the income level at which Social Security benefits become taxable from roughly $25,000-$32,000 to $100,000, cutting income taxes for many middle-income retirees. The bill was sent to the Ways and Means Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Middle-income retirees, who would pay income tax on less of their Social Security benefits; future Social Security recipients generally, because the new tax on earnings above $300,000 would extend the trust fund's life; and Social Security beneficiaries overall, since the program's financing gap would narrow.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Middle-income retirees and Social Security's future

how_it_helps.text: The bill applies the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax (employee and employer shares combined) to annual income above $300,000, keeping the existing tax on wages up to the yearly cap unchanged [S2][S3].

It raises to $100,000 the income threshold above which Social Security benefits count as taxable income, so retirees below that level would pay no income tax on their benefits; a general-fund appropriation would hold the trust funds financially whole for the lost revenue [S2][S3].

It includes earnings above $300,000 in the Social Security benefit formula at a 3% factor, so very high earners get a small benefit credit in return for the new tax, and it applies only to people first eligible after 2017 [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Individuals with wage or self-employment income above $300,000 a year, who would pay Social Security tax on everything above that level with no cap; and very high-income retirees, who would still pay tax on benefits. The bill's tax cut for moderate retirees is paid for out of general federal revenue.

drawbacks.text: The tax applies in a donut: income between the roughly $127,200 cap and $300,000 stays untaxed, so the bill spares upper-middle earners and lands only on the very top [S2][S3].
The benefit-formula credit for the new tax is only 3% of excess earnings, so high earners pay substantially more than they get back — the financing gain comes from that imbalance [S2][S3].

Raising the benefit-tax exclusion to $100,000 reduces federal income tax revenue, and the bill covers the trust funds' loss by appropriating general Treasury money, meaning all federal taxpayers indirectly absorb that cost [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall almost entirely on the top slice of earners and on a modest general-revenue offset, while the direct benefit to middle-income retirees is immediate and the solvency benefit to all beneficiaries is real, though the donut design and the small 3% benefit credit limit how much new revenue it raises relative to a full lifting of the cap.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until Congress ended in January 2019, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Charlie Crist introduced the Save Social Security Act of 2017 on March 20, 2017 [S1][S5].
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee the same day, and the bill took no further action in the record for the rest of the 115th Congress [S5].
It had one cosponsor, a Democrat, and no committee action or vote ever occurred before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People earning over $300,000 a year, whose Social Security tax stays capped, and the committee leadership that kept the status quo on Social Security financing without facing a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners who kept the payroll tax cap

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — after referral on March 20, 2017

sides.party_line_note: Only two House Democrats are on record supporting the bill; no Republicans sponsored or cosponsored it, and no votes were ever recorded, so opposition was silent but total.

industries.note: They would pay the 12.4% Social Security tax on all income above $300,000 with no upper cap, with only a small 3% benefit credit in return. The revenue would extend Social Security's solvency, which the rest of earners fund on their full wages up to the cap.
The bill explicitly covers self-employment income above $300,000, so high-earning owners and independent professionals would owe both the employer and employee shares on the excess [S3].

Retirees with other income would still pay income tax on up to 85% of their benefits under the new structure, while retirees under the $100,000 threshold get an exemption — the tax on benefits shifts onto higher-income seniors [S2][S3].
Retirees with income under $100,000 would pay no income tax on their Social Security benefits, a direct tax cut that the general fund absorbs [S2][S3].
